svg.font-family: Inter, Segoe UI, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
svg.title: Figure 1. What mobile operational security guidance covers, and where it actually fails
svg.desc: Two columns. The left lists the threats that most mobile operational security material spends its length on: fake cell towers, brief physical access by a stranger, forced unlock at a border, and targeted surveillance. The right lists the failures that actually occur for working security professionals: client screenshots synchronising to a personal photo library, client contacts entering a personal address book, work accounts on a device shared with family, and engagement locations recorded in photograph metadata. A band below observes that the right column carries contractual and legal consequences, requires no attacker at all, and receives a fraction of the coverage.
svg.text: Figure 1: The Column That Gets Written About, and the Column That Happens
Both columns are real. Only one of them is likely to happen to you this year, and it is not the interesting one.
most of the length, most of the excitement

g.text: Fake cell towers
Real, deployed, and worth understanding. Also largely
defeated by using encrypted messaging, which you do anyway.
Brief physical access by a stranger
Real, and the hardware and firmware protections in Lesson 5.1
and 5.3 are the answer rather than tape over the ports.
Forced unlock at a border
Real, common, and the legal structure matters more than the
technique. Figure 3 covers it precisely.
Targeted surveillance by a capable adversary
Real for a small number of people, and the honest advice for
them is a specialist, not a lesson.
None of this is wrong. It is disproportionate.

svg.text: no attacker required, and rarely mentioned

g.text: A screenshot of a finding, in a synchronised library
You photograph a console, a diagram, a whiteboard. The photo
library uploads it. Lesson 5.1 Tier 2, holding client data.
Client contacts in a personal address book
Which synchronises, and which you granted to applications
years ago. Their names, roles and numbers, not yours.
A work account on a device the household uses
Notifications on a lock screen in a shared room. A tablet
signed into the same account. Nobody attacked anything.
The engagement itself, in photograph metadata
Coordinates and timestamps recording which organisation
hired you and when. Lesson 1.3, arriving through a camera.
Every one of these is a confidentiality breach.

svg.text: Why the right column deserves the length, and gets a footnote instead

g.text: It requires no attacker. Nothing has to go wrong for these to happen. They are the default behaviour of a correctly working phone.
The consequences are contractual, not technical. A confidentiality clause does not distinguish between a breach and a synchronisation setting.
And it is boring, which is the actual reason it gets a footnote. Nobody writes an exciting section about turning off photo sync on a work phone.

svg.text: So this lesson does the right column first and at length, then covers the left column accurately rather than dramatically.
If you only do one thing from this lesson: separate the device or the profile that touches client work from the one that holds your life.
That single change closes most of the right column, and no amount of counter-surveillance technique closes any of it.
